title: Critical points, stationary points, and monotonicity
section: Curve Sketching ▷ Properties of the first derivative
terms: critical point; stationary point; increasing function; decreasing function; first-derivative test.

exposition.text:
An interior domain point is critical if its derivative is zero or does not exist; it is stationary
when its derivative is zero. A positive derivative throughout an interval implies strict increase
there, and a negative derivative implies strict decrease. These are interval conclusions, not
claims about global behavior from a derivative value at a single point.
The first-derivative test classifies a critical point by a sign change: positive to negative gives a
local maximum; negative to positive gives a local minimum; no sign change need give neither.
Include nondifferentiable domain points, but do not count excluded points such as poles as
′
critical points of the function. A repeated factor of even multiplicity in f usually does not
change its sign; odd multiplicity does.

question.text:
′ 2 3
A differentiable function satisfies f (x) = x (x − 1) (x + 2). At which points does f have local
extrema?
(A) x = 0 only (B) x = −2, 0 only
(C) x = 0, 1 only (D) x = −2, 1 only
(E) x = −2, 0, 1

solution.text:
′
The sign of f is positive on (−∞, −2), negative on (−2, 0) and (0, 1), and positive on
(1, ∞). Thus −2 is a local maximum and 1 a local minimum, while the double zero at 0 is
stationary without an extremum.

question.text:
2/3
For f(x) = |x| (x − 2), which statement about x = 0 is correct?
(A) It is a differentiable local minimum.
(B) It is a differentiable local maximum.
(C) It is a nondifferentiable local maximum.
(D) It is a nondifferentiable local minimum.
(E) It is not a critical point.

solution.text:
f(0) = 0 and f(x) < 0 for every sufficiently small nonzero x, so zero is a strict local maxi-
2/3
mum. The quotient f (h)/h = |h| (h − 2)/h has unbounded one-sided values, so no finite
derivative exists.

question.text:
′ ′
A differentiable f : R → R has f (x) ≥ 0 everywhere, and f (x) = 0 at only countably many
points. Which must hold?
′
(A) f (x) > 0 everywhere.
(B) f is strictly increasing.
(C) f is constant on some interval.
(D) f has a strict local maximum.
(E) f is bounded.

solution.text:
The mean value theorem makes f nondecreasing. If f(a) = f(b) for some a < b, monotonic-
ity would force it to be constant throughout [a, b], making its derivative zero at every point
of the uncountable interval (a, b). This contradicts the stated zero set. Strict increase does
not require a strictly positive derivative at every point.

question.text:
How many stationary points does f(x) = x + 1/x have on its natural real domain?
(A) 1 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 2 (E) 0

solution.text:
2
The derivative is 1 − 1/x , which vanishes at x = ±1. The excluded point zero is not a sta-
tionary point.
